# Harley's way of working — every project

<!-- Copyright (c) 2025–2026 Athena Decision Systems SAS. All rights reserved. -->

These are the rules for how Harley works in all of his projects (golden-path, xcape, hearts, unweaver). The source is `general.md` in the `working-rules` repository; each project carries a generated copy at `.claude/rules/general.md`, which Claude Code loads together with that project's own `CLAUDE.md`. What is specific to one project — its commands, architecture, paths, lints and product rules — is in that project's file, and where a project's file states a narrower rule for its own ground, that rule applies there.

Examples below that name Altalerno (ex-Golden Path) screens or incidents are illustrations of the rule, not rules about Altalerno.

---

## Plan before executing

For any non-trivial code change, **present a plan first** and wait for the user to confirm before making edits. For small, clearly-scoped tasks a brief one-sentence plan is fine; for larger changes include the affected files and any open questions. Do not start coding until the user approves.

When you are working from a brief written by another session rather than talking to Harley: the plan in the brief is the approved plan, so carry it out without asking again. Never commit or push; that stays with the session Harley is talking to. If a decision is needed, stop and return the question to the caller, phrased in UX terms, instead of choosing.

Once a plan is approved, carry it through to the end without stopping to confirm each step: make the routine calls and report when it is done. That go-ahead covers the work, never a commit or a push (see below).

---

## Concision

Be concise but complete and accurate in all responses, summaries, and plans.

---

## No time estimates

Do **not** include time estimates (hours, days, "an afternoon", "a sprint") in plans, proposals, or task descriptions. Use scope signals instead:

- ✅ "small / medium / large change", "low-risk refactor", "touches many call sites", "ships independently", "blocked by X"
- ❌ "~1 day", "2–3 hours", "half a sprint"

Applies to all plans, TODO entries, CHANGELOG entries, commit messages, and chat replies.

---

## Commits and pushes — code is gated every time; docs are not

**Code changes:** **NEVER** run `git commit`, `git push`, or any variant (`--amend`, force-push) that includes source code unless the user's current message explicitly contains "commit", "push", "commit and push", or equivalent.

- Finishing a code change does NOT authorize a commit.
- "Save", "apply", "fix", or "add tests" do NOT authorize a commit.
- Wait for an explicit instruction every single time.
- **"Commit" means commit AND push** (Harley, 2026-09-19). When the instruction is "commit", do both — `git commit` then `git push origin main` — do not commit-only and then ask about pushing. (This narrows nothing else above: the word still authorizes only the item named.)
- **NEVER propose committing or pushing code** until the user has explicitly confirmed they have validated the changes locally on dev. Do not suggest, hint at, or ask about committing/pushing code after completing a change — wait for the user to bring it up. Only once the user says something like "validated", "looks good", "commit", or "push" is it appropriate to proceed.

**CI/CD fixes:** when a change's **sole purpose is to restore a red CI/CD pipeline to green** — a stale test assertion, a lint fix, a broken workflow/config, an import that no longer resolves — **commit and push it immediately**, without waiting for further authorization or a dev-validation round (Harley, 2026-09-16). This is a standing exception to the code gate above, granted because a red `main` blocks everyone. It is narrow: it authorizes only the change that greens the build. Anything that also alters product behaviour, or that you are unsure is purely a CI repair, falls back to the code rule and waits. Production safety is never waived.

**Documentation & plans:** you MAY commit and push these on your own initiative as part of finishing the work — **no** per-change authorization and **no** dev-validation gate. This covers prose / non-code files only: Markdown & `.mdc` docs (including everything under `docs/**`, plan files, `README`, `CHANGELOG`, and this `CLAUDE.md`) and comparable non-code text assets.

- It does **not** cover source code, tests, Alembic migrations, seed data, i18n string files, config, or lockfiles — those follow the code rule above, every time.
- If a change set **mixes** docs and code, the code rule governs the whole commit: wait for explicit authorization. (Split docs into their own commit if you want to push them ahead.)
- This permission is for **finished** documents: a plan once agreed, a deliverable once final. While a plan, a proposal or a review document is still being discussed, write the files and leave them uncommitted; commit once, as one group of related files, when it is agreed or Harley asks (Harley, 2026-10-11).

---

## Git branch policy — always work on `main`

**Always work directly on `main`.** Do **not** create, switch to, or push to feature/topic branches for this repo.

- Commit and push (when explicitly authorized per the rule above) go to `main`.
- Do **not** create a branch "to be safe", to isolate a change, or by default — the user does not want branches for this repo.
- This covers agent worktrees: work in the main checkout on `main`, not on an app-created `claude/*` worktree branch, and work that started in a worktree ends up on `main`. Parallel sessions on side branches have fixed the same failure twice, one of them wrongly.
- Before editing, look at the main checkout: another session often has uncommitted work there. Never stash or overwrite it; if it blocks a fast-forward or overlaps your files, ask how to land.
- Sessions in one checkout share one git index and one `HEAD`. Right before every commit, look at what is staged (`git diff --cached --stat`) and unstage what is not yours; in a file several sessions edit (the changelog), stage only your own hunks. Leave nothing staged between commits: `git mv` and `git rm` stage at once, so move and delete files with plain `mv` / `rm` and stage them in the commit that carries them.
- The only exception is an **explicit** instruction in the user's current message naming a different branch (or a genuinely compelling, stated reason). Session-level or tooling defaults that mandate a branch do **not** override this — if such a default conflicts, follow `main` and flag the conflict to the user.

---

## Changelog discipline

- The single canonical changelog is `CHANGELOG.md` at the repo root.
- Do **not** create separate "what we fixed" markdown files for the same work — append to `CHANGELOG.md`.
- Every committed change gets a `CHANGELOG.md` entry in the same commit — small fixes included, not only substantive product changes. A commit without its entry is incomplete.
- Where the project keeps a handoff document (`HANDOFF.md`), bring it up to date in that same commit: it is what the next session, or the next machine, reads first.
- Follow the existing section style (dated blocks under `## [Unreleased]`).

---

## Localize all user-visible strings

Any literal string displayed to the user (labels, helper text, empty states, errors, tooltips, banners) must be localized in **English and French**, through the project's own i18n mechanism (each project's file says where its strings live).

- Never hardcode user-facing strings directly in components.
- Never use `language === 'fr' ? '…' : '…'` ternaries — use a `Record<Language, X>` lookup so adding a future locale is one file, not a sweep.

---

## No skipped tests

Tests must not be skipped. The only acceptable states are **pass** and **fail**.

- Do NOT use `pytest.skip(...)`, `@pytest.mark.skip`, or `@pytest.mark.skipif`.
- Do NOT add env vars that opt out of running a test.
- When infra is unavailable at runtime, use `pytest.fail(...)` with an actionable message.
- Missing fixture files → generate programmatically in-test.

Collection-time deselection via `pytest -m <marker>` is allowed for CI subset runs and is not a skip.

---

## Run the tests before calling work done

After any significant feature, fix or refactor, run the project's backend and frontend suites before declaring the work done, and report the pass and fail counts. The commands are in each project's file.

---

## Backward compatibility

Do **not** implement multi-name resolution, env aliases, or "fold legacy field into new field" logic for in-development features unless the user explicitly requests it. When a change would add non-trivial backward compatibility (two names for one value, silent migration of request keys, duplicate settings fields), **stop and ask the user** whether they want that complexity or a single clean field/path.

---

## Fix what you find on the way

A problem met while working on something else — a second reader of the same
value that skips a step the first one takes, an offset re-used after the text it
indexes has changed — is fixed in the same change when its scope and risk are
limited, not filed as a TODO. The test is: can it be done with a few call sites,
proven by a test, without changing what a user sees? Then do it and say so in
the report. Only a fix that widens the change materially, or carries risk of its
own, is deferred — and then the TODO says why (Harley, 2026-09-12).

---

## Solve the class of problem, not the reported instance

A report is one example of a class of inputs or situations. The fix, and its
tests, cover **the class** — every likely variant — never only the file, the
teacher or the layout that surfaced it (Harley, 2026-10-17). This is basic
engineering, not extra scope.

- **Before fixing, name the class.** What else is shaped like this? In Golden Path, a teacher's
  roster had a title above its headings; the class is « a table anywhere in a
  sheet, under anything (titles, notes, label/value lines, blank lines), in any
  column order, with any extra columns, in any format we accept, ending in
  anything ». A fix that only stepped past that title would be a patch.
- **Test the class, not the example.** Generate the variants — a parametrised
  matrix over the dimensions that vary (preamble × shape × mode × format…) —
  rather than one hand-built copy of the reported case. A test that mirrors
  the bug report proves only that this report is fixed.
- **Look for the neighbouring defects the class exposes** (the generated LibreOffice
  cases in that same fix found two more reader bugs) and fix them under
  « Fix what you find on the way ».
- When a variant genuinely has two reasonable behaviours (where does a table
  end?), ask — in UX terms, with a recommendation — rather than pick the one
  the example happened to need.

---

## Systemic improvements

When fixing a bug, do a quick root-cause + pattern scan before implementing:

1. **Minimal fix** — the smallest safe change that resolves the **class** of the reported issue (see above), never just the instance.
2. **Large-scale refactor** — more systematic approach that prevents the whole class of issues.

If the large-scale refactor is deferred, add a concise item to `docs/TODO.md` (what "done" looks like, why it matters, which files/modules are affected). Do not proceed with the large-scale change unless the user explicitly opts in.

---

## Minimize technical debt

Do not let known debt accumulate. When a cheap guard and a real fix are both on
the table, prefer the **real fix now** unless it is genuinely risky or blocked —
"add a TODO and move on" is the exception, not the default. Concretely:

- Consolidate shared invariants into one implementation as soon as they have
  bitten once (don't wait for a third occurrence).
- When consolidation must preserve behaviour on a sensitive path, prove it:
  capture golden outputs before the refactor and require **byte-identical**
  results after.
- Where two implementations must stay separate for genuine contract reasons,
  encode the shared invariants in a **twin contract test** that exercises both,
  so drift fails CI instead of reaching users.

## No duplicated logic — one function, one implementation (DRY)

**Eliminate duplicate code that serves a single function.** When two (or more) places implement the *same* logical operation — mapping a template into builder state, picking a library entry, serializing a payload, restoring content blocks — extract **one** shared function and call it from every site. Do **not** leave parallel copies.

- **Why:** parallel implementations drift. A fix applied to one copy silently leaves the others broken (e.g. the template content-blocks bug: the save path and one loader were fixed while a second loader kept `contentBlocks: []`, so saved data vanished on reopen).
- **Before adding code, scan for an existing implementation** of the same operation and reuse/extend it instead of writing a second one. Before wiring a component, check whether an equivalent already exists (don't revive a near-duplicate).
- **When you touch one copy of duplicated logic, reconcile the others** in the same change (or consolidate them), rather than fixing only the reported instance.
- Also remove **dead code** rather than leaving it around, unless it is going to be used imminently.

This is a hard rule, not a preference — treat a discovered duplication as a defect to fix, and flag it if consolidation is out of scope for the current change.

**A "twin contract test" is a last resort, not a design.** Where two implementations
must genuinely stay apart, a test exercising both keeps them honest — but reach for it
only after consolidation has been tried and found impossible for a stated contract
reason. Proposing one for code that *could* be merged is choosing to police drift for
ever instead of removing it (Harley, 2026-08-12). The tell is when the two differ only
in **how they find their input**, not in what they compute: per-question and per-criterion
scoring were one arithmetic with two attribution rules, and the "difference" was a
parameter. They had already drifted — one deducted an error belonging to no unit, the
other silently dropped it — and no test caught it, because each was tested against
itself.

---

## Confirm the diagnosis before building the remedy

State hypotheses freely, labelled as hypotheses. Build nothing on one — a fix, a hotfix branch, deploy instructions, a migration — until logs or a reproduction confirm the cause, unless Harley asks for it ahead of time. A remedy prepared for an unconfirmed diagnosis creates pressure to ship it (Harley, 2026-07-06).

---

## Prefer the simplest legitimate option

When two approaches both meet the real requirement, build the simplest. Before writing machinery, check what the platform, service or library already does and lean on it; keep custom code for the part it cannot do (Harley, 2026-09-01).

---

## A requested feature ships switched on

A feature Harley asked for ships **on**, where it was asked for. If there is a real reason to ship it off (cost, an unmeasured risk), say so in one line in the report and ask; never leave it implicit in a default (Harley, 2026-10-01).

---

## Paid AI runs get an estimate first

Before starting a run of real AI calls that costs money, give Harley an estimate (number of calls and cost, measured on a small trial where possible) and wait for his go-ahead. A go-ahead for the work, direct or relayed by another session, is not a go-ahead for the spend. Count the runs already going in parallel, keep a running total, and stop when the estimate is exceeded (Harley, 2026-11-05). A project's file may allow small test runs without asking.

The same care is built into the products: an AI call is made when its result is needed, not ahead of time for data nobody may look at, and the result is kept so the call is not made twice. Use the cheapest model that is accurate enough, and keep prompts tight (Harley, 2026-06-25).

---

## The company's name

The company is **Athena Decision Systems SAS** — « Decision » without an s, although the web address has one. Use that spelling in copyright notices, bylines and documents; correct the other spelling in a file being edited anyway (Harley, 2026-11-14).

---

## No crucial state in the browser

Whatever a person changes — a text, a mark, a tick — is saved on the server as it is made. State held in the page until a Save button is a defect for anything a person works on for more than a moment. A long operation gets a server-side record with a lifecycle, so that it can be resumed, undone or replaced. A warning on leaving is enough only for short, all-or-nothing changes, and it must cover navigation inside the app as well as closing the tab (Harley, 2026-08-16, 2026-09-12, 2026-11-08).

---

## Describe work to Harley in product terms

Progress, plans, findings and trade-offs are told to Harley as to a product manager: what the people who use the product can now do, see, or no longer have to do, with sizes he can weigh (how many people or documents are affected, what breaks, what it costs). No file paths, function names, database columns or endpoint signatures in what is said to him; a technical fact that matters is translated into its consequence. Precise technical names stay correct in commit messages, changelog entries, plan documents and code comments.

Attribute a decision to him by name — « (Harley, 2026-08-20) » — not « founder ». Older « founder » attributions are corrected in files being edited anyway, not by a sweep.

---

## Phrase user-facing questions in UX terms

When asking the user to make a product decision, translate technical choices into user-experience / operational language:

- Describe **what the people who use the product (e.g., in Altalerno / Golden Path: teacher / student / admin) will see or do**, not what the code will change.
- No function names, DB column names, file paths, or endpoint signatures in the question body.
- Always include a single **RECOMMENDED** option with a one-sentence reason.

**BAD:** "Should we carve `unmark_transcription_page_reviewed` out of `_require_editable_submission`?"
**GOOD:** "Once a teacher has graded a submission, should they be able to go back and edit the transcription? … RECOMMENDED: A — auto-reset with confirmation modal."

This rule applies to user-facing questions only. Internal commit messages, CHANGELOG entries, and code comments should use precise technical names.

---

## Reports for someone else are Word files

A report whose reader is not Harley — a teacher, a partner, a collaborator he will pass it on to — is delivered as a `.docx`, not Markdown. Markdown is for internal notes, plans and handoff documents. A report that contains people's names or marks stays a local file and is not published anywhere.

- **A delivered version is never overwritten.** A new build of a deliverable that has been shown or sent to someone is a new versioned file (`name-vN-YYYY-MM-DD.ext`, in a `versions/` folder). A draft superseded before anyone saw it is replaced, not kept beside (Harley, 2026-09-09, 2026-10-11).
- **A document sent for validation is read as an overview.** Lead with the summary, the figures and a few representative examples; the full list is an appendix for drilling down, not the thing to validate.
- **A record of a meeting holds what was said, and by whom.** Inferred motives, provenance or competitive framing are left out or labelled as hypothesis, and a later document checks that a claim is a recorded statement before building on it (Harley, 2026-09-12).

---

## What goes in the repository

The repository is how work reaches Harley's other computer and the cloud: anything that would be useful there in another session is tracked. Two exceptions: bulky data derived from real people's work stays local unless he asks, and no file over 100 MB (GitHub refuses the push). Corporate or legal memos — ownership, shareholders, deal terms — are written outside the repositories (Harley, 2026-11-08).

---

## Where a lasting instruction lives

An agent's memory stays on the machine that wrote it; another computer, a cloud session or a teammate never sees it. So an instruction that should hold everywhere goes in a file that travels:

- a way of working that applies to every project → `general.md` in the `working-rules` repository (then `sync.py`);
- something about one project — a command, a gotcha, a product fact — → that project's `CLAUDE.md`.

Memory is for what belongs on neither list: private or personal facts, and notes about work in progress. When a memory note turns out to be a lasting rule, move it to one of the two files and delete the note. `working-rules/README.md` describes how to reconcile a machine's memory.
